utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. Good morning. I merely wish to inform you that I submitted this morning our exhibits. We have three binders, and we shall be told by the registrar if more copies are needed. And P11.18 and 8.8 already exist. We merely wish to tender P11.18, that he could not recognise anything in the town of Mostar, or the photograph, as you will remember, the Ministry of Defence, and the photograph of Doljani where he merely drew an arrow in the direction of the mosque. That is all. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. In respect of 11.18 and 8.8, counsel is right; the witness simply didn't recognise anything on those exhibits, which are already in evidence anyway. So I think the evidence is the witness's testimony that he didn't recognise anything on them. It seems to me pointless to, once again, offer the same exhibits, because the witness didn't recognise anything on them. And so I don't think it's -- it just doesn't seem to be necessary to re-offer the same exhibits which, as I think the Court has indicated, are already in evidence. The evidence is the fact that the witness didn't recognise anything on them. So I guess that's our response. We don't see the need, and we therefore object to whatever it is that counsel's proposing now in respect to those two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in certain jurisdictions, if the witness did not recognise anything on certain exhibits, it is the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. But I think the evidence is the witness's words, which can be linked to the exhibits because those exhibits are already admitted into evidence. And maybe I don't understand precisely what counsel's intentions are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Since the Exhibits 11.18 and 8.8 have been admitted into the evidence already, so when we evaluate all those evidence, we will take into account of this fact, that the witness did not recognise anything on those exhibits. So it seems to me that it does not matter whether it has been readmitted or not as the Defence evidence or not. It's not that important. But anyway, to be fair to the Defence counsel, we'll have those two photos admitted as evidence, as Defence evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could make two additional comments in respect of the Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: On further reflection, we withdraw our objection to the judgement from the German proceedings. We don't have an objection to that being admitted into evidence. But we did want to suggest, this is a rather voluminous set of exhibits. It's true that they were received, I believe, by the Defence from the Prosecutor in disclosure during the pre-trial phase of the case. We have not received, however, that exhibit from the Defence marked as Defence exhibits, and we just want to make sure that we're going to receive those exhibits as Defence exhibits back from the Defence, even though, in some sense, we have possession of those documents throughout our investigative files. But we would like to have them from the Defence as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And how about those previous statements made by the witness? I think those three binders, or whatever amount of binders, is composed of three parts. One is the judgement. The other is all the letters. The third one is the previous statements by this witness. I haven't seen those -- I haven't received those binders yet at this moment. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that I stated the Prosecution position yesterday in respect of statements of the witness, that is, the statements that he made to investigators either of the Office of the Prosecutor or the German authorities, that in our view those may be considered by the Trial Chamber as they may go to the credibility of the witness or as they may indicate or contain inconsistencies with his testimony in the courtroom but that the statements themselves are not evidence; otherwise, we could just simply tender all our witness statements and not call any witnesses any more. So with that qualification, we don't object to the Trial Chamber having those and considering those statements for that limited purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. May it please Your Honours and my learned colleague, Mr. Stringer, we will definitely deliver to the Prosecution a copy. I have a meeting with Madam Registrar at the lunch hour to get all this straightened out and get the proper numbers. I would just state that we attempted to make all copies last night, but the copy machine in Defence counsel room broke. Nobody was there to fix it. Nothing works in Defence counsel room. So that's why we don't have them all today. We will settle this matter at lunch hour, and we will give the Prosecutor copies of all those. And Your Honour, Mr. President, you're right, there will be three -- they are in one binder, but it's the letters, the statements, and then the German judgement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. This Trial Chamber will make the decisions after we have received all those documents submitted by the Defence counsel. So, Mr. Scott, are we ready for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour. Good morning. I might say -- well, one thing about the witness, by way of introduction, and one other item, if I can take just one more moment before calling the witness. Probably showed up in front of Your Honours yesterday afternoon - might have been a bit mysterious, although I'm sure you probably figured it out for yourselves - we tendered, the Prosecution tendered, yesterday a further updated witness order for the next -- extending the time out into mid-November. We've done that, as you know, on a - if I can use the word - rolling basis. There has been a full list at various times, and we have tried to update those lists in the best we can, absolutely the most accurate information, several weeks out, and then we've been providing those as we go, so that, roughly speaking, we hope to stay about 30 days, approximately 30 days, ahead of where we are. So that was tendered to both the Defence and Your Honours yesterday. I might say, Your Honours, just - I have said this to the Defence, and I'm not here to debate that this morning - but I've indicated to the Defence of course we will expect similar treatment from the Defence; that is, 30 days' notice prior to their witnesses being called. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, your remarks remind me of your motion about the videolink witnesses. At this moment, we are expecting a written response from the Defence counsel. Then we will make the decisions. As you know, at late part of November, this Trial Chamber will have certain other obligations, so we hope we could arrange those videolink witnesses either in the beginning of November or in beginning of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would think at the moment - I would have to say in candour, I think the beginning of November is unrealistic. I think, given the way these things work, in my experience, they cannot be put in place that quickly. There are motions. There are official requests pending to the United States government. In fact, some additional information is just being sent out by Prosecutor Del Ponte today. So I can't honestly stand here and tell the Court that early November is realistic. I think late November is probably more realistic, or early December, and all that of course depends on the continuing trial schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in regards to the videolink, we believe -- Mr. Scott and Mr. Stringer and Defence counsel believe that we have an agreement. I'm going to speak with Mr. Scott and Mr. Stringer before the end of today. I believe we have an agreement that we do not object to this procedure, with some conditions that they don't object to. So then if we have the agreement, we just -- well, it will be up to Your Honours whether you approve that agreement. But I don't think there is going to be much argument between Prosecutor and Defence counsel on the videolink. It will just be the timing and whether Your Honours are going to abide by what we agree to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Which means that you're not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We will write that, Your Honour, if you want us to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You'll submit the written submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sure. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And be aware of your time schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We will do it promptly, Your Honour. There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So, Mr. Scott, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are. As the next witness will be testifying in open session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't see Mr. Krsnik standing. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honours. I will not take too much of your time. I cannot, however, disregard one factor, that is, that my learned friend expects also the Defence will submit its list of witnesses within 30 days. Your Honours, the Defence was to have the final list 30 days earlier so that we could -- that is the purpose of it. We could get ready for this defence. But now we have started, and we have practically no time to have supper - if you will pardon my expression - we have to work so much. And had we had the final witness list 30 days before the beginning of this trial, then the Defence would have considered it fair and just. After this, Your Honours, we all know very well that we received the final list of witnesses two days before the trial. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, to my understanding, the Prosecutor only submitted lists, that is, in the order of appearance, for the 30 days, and I think he already disclosed all the lists of the witness to you for you to prepare your cross-examination. Is that true, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't want to belabour that this morning. If there's any confusion about this, I would ask the Chamber to calendar a separate time when the witnesses aren't present, and I will be happy to take counsel and the Chamber through each piece of correspondence over the past several months. It is not correct or fair for Mr. Krsnik to stand up and make that statement. He knows it not to be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are not going to have a debate on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope you have your witness as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He is ready to go, Your Honour, this moment. I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the witness comes in, would you please brief us with the relevancy in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness will be testifying in open session, so I will go ahead and state his name for the record. It's Seid Smajkic. He is the Mufti of Mostar, which is a very senior Islamic church official. His testimony will be relevant to the background portions of the indictment, paragraphs 9 through 11; general allegations, paragraph 21, count 1; persecutions, paragraph 26 and 27, counts 9 to 12; torture and great suffering, paragraph 46 and 47, count 18; forcible transfer, paragraphs 53, counts 19 and 20; destruction of property, count 22; destruction of religious institutions, paragraph 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, you may sit down. Examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Smajkic. Would you state your full name for the record and spell your last name for the reporters, please.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Good morning. I am Seid Smajkic, S-m-a-j-k-i-c.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, you were born in 1947 and spent most of your life in Mostar or the Mostar region; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that since approximately 1980, you have been what is called the Mufti -- and I will ask you some questions about that in a moment -- you have been the Mufti of Mostar, or for Mostar? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please describe briefly for the Chamber what -- who or what a Mufti is and what functions and responsibilities you have in that position.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It is the chief cleric in an area covering all the religious activities in a region or, in this particular case, in Herzegovina, and beyond it. A Mufti will oversee the religious life, religious activities, the work of religious schools, celebrations of religious holidays, activities related to the organisation of all affairs of concern to the Islamic religious community. This is for the Chamber and for you; this equals the rank of a Bishop in the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And you have held this position, as I said a moment ago, since 1980; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: From 1975, I was first the acting Mufti. And as of 1980, yes, I became a Mufti officially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned this as part of your answer, but so it is clear, would you please tell the Chamber your geographic area of responsibility or, we might say, jurisdiction, please.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, if we start from the north, it's Konjic, Prozor, Jablanica, Mostar, Ljubuski, Tomislavgrad, Livno, Glamoc, Capljina, Stolac, and Neum. And now, in view of the present division in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, now we also have Trebinje, Nevesinje, Bileca, Gacko, Ljubinje, which are in the Republica Srpska. This whole area is under my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you said earlier, I believe -- and again -- we might just know that area or, roughly speaking, call that, in fact, Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to pick up on a couple of particular areas of responsibility which will come up probably later in your testimony, what is your function or role in relation to other church officials, if I can put it this way? And if I'm saying it incorrectly, please forgive me. But lower church officials, local religious leaders, Islamic religious leaders, what is your responsibility toward them?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Every municipality has its own territorial institution. There are the authorities of the Islamic community with a certain number of Imams. Civilians may also participate in the authorities and be responsible for property, law, real estate affairs, but the religious life is in the hands of the Imams. These are lower organisational units to the municipal level, and I am their superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have some responsibility for the -- for overseeing these individuals, on the one hand, and also receiving information from them? I mean, if you will, communications up and down with these lower church officials.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, from below, above. And that is from above going down, and from below going up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly, then, in closing on this description of your roles and responsibilities, what is your responsibility towards the church -- the physical structures and facilities of the Islamic church in your region? What responsibilities do you have in that regard?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The municipal administrative bodies of the Islamic community are responsible for all the practical matters dealing with land use for religious needs, and I am referring to purely religious objects, that is, houses of worship, mosques, then educational institutions where children and youth are instructed in the basics of Islam. We also have our official premises, our offices, and also official residences of Imams. In other words, at the municipal level, they are the ones who shape, who run the religious life and are responsible to me in higher instances for their programmes, for their activities, and for the protection of religious objects, among other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I think that's a full account on that matter. In terms of the mosques themselves, let me ask you a couple of questions. If a local community of Islamic faith, wishes -- for instance, if they wanted to build a mosque in their local area, would you be involved in that in the sense of would you have to give some sort of approvals or be involved in that decision-making process?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And putting it the other way around, if I can put it that way, if a mosque in a particular area was destroyed, would that typically come -- in the area of your responsibility, would that come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, I'm going to jump -- go rather quickly to April of 1992, and so as not to do that in a complete vacuum, I have about four or five leading questions simply by way of background to bring us to that point, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, is it correct that in approximately early 1992, what was then sometimes referred to as the Serb and Montenegrin army took control, in whole or in part, of the area of Mostar, against both Croats and Muslims or Bosniaks in that region?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That took place in early April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And, Mr. Smajkic, you've heard what I said to the President, so I'm going to tell you now -- and these questions may seem very broad and generic to you, and admittedly they are, but for these purposes, I'm just citing -- asking to you confirm some broad background matters, if you will. In April 1992, as you just said, is it correct, then, that armed conflict broke out and intensified, in fact, during that April to June 1992 period?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We can even say that prior to 1st of April, there were sporadic clashes. However, as of April, these conflicts and clashes did intensify, and this went on into early June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, again by way of introduction, that during the spring of 1992, and perhaps even earlier, the Bosniak community and the Croat community were, to varying degrees and extents, working together or trying to take steps together in opposition to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally in this series of questions, is it correct that as of about the middle of June 1992, the Serbs withdrew from the city of Mostar itself to some of the mountain areas in the vicinity of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This took place between the 16th and the 18th of June, 1992 - yes, that is correct - due to joint efforts of the HVO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I was -- that's one of the next things I was going to come to, Mr. Smajkic. There has been some suggestion at times, that this Chamber has heard, that it was only the HVO, that is, the Croat side, that was responsible or had the role of expelling, if you will, Serb forces from the city of Mostar. Is that true, from your experience and what you know?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I was a witness of all these events because I was in the city of Mostar at that time, which at that time was surrounded by what we termed Serbo-Montenegrin aggressor, and I do know that the HVO or the Croatian side has frequently pointed out their superiority when it relates to the defence of the city, and they also marginalised the role of Bosniaks in this defence. However, I can be -- I'll be very open and frank in saying that the most casualties were actually on the Bosniak side, and that, in fact, with their units, which at that time admittedly were part of the HVO, were part of the force which helped push the Serbs out of Mostar, even though later on, after all these events, in retrospect, we can assess that that was some -- that is, it is my assessment that this expulsion of Serbs from Mostar was really a form of agreement. However, we can go into further detail in discussing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we will get to that. But not to leave that hanging, perhaps maybe getting just a bit ahead of ourselves - but since you've taken us there - when you say that it was -- the expulsion of the Serbs from Mostar was really a form of agreement, would you please explain what you mean to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Knowing what forces the Serbs and Montenegrins and the JNA had in the Neretva River valley, to a person who is impartial would find it hard to believe that such a break-through would have taken place in such a short period of time, and that such forces could have been pushed out of not only the city of Mostar but from the wider area of the Neretva River valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you again, just try to finish up a bit more clarity on that. If they weren't expelled, if they were not removed or withdrew by force, as a result of force, how is it that you're saying that they did withdraw; that is, the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Naturally, there were combat operations conducted there, and people did lose lives, but in such an operation, which was like lightning, it would have been impossible to force these forces to redeploy to those features. I know that during a period of time, there were certain arrangements, arrangements between the Serbian and Croatian sides regarding the city of Mostar, because I myself took place in one of these incidents, perhaps I should call them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's leave it at that for the moment, and we will probably be back to that in a few minutes. But with that background now, let me direct your attention to a particular event or a document. Do you recall that on approximately the 29th of April, 1992, a document was signed by various members of the Croat community and the Bosniak community in connection with the defence of the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I am completely familiar, and thank you for refreshing my memory on this. So many events took place, and from this distance it is hard to put them all together in one time line, without having the aid of documents. I am familiar with that document and with its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me at this time ask for the usher's assistance, and to the Chamber as a whole, if it hasn't been done so already. There is a packet of exhibits that have been prepared, Mr. President, that will be used with this witness. I think they've been given to the Defence already; I hope. But I think for the witness and for the Chamber, please, if they could be distributed. They are, generally speaking, in both chronological and numerical order. I say "generally." There are some exceptions in which you may find that a document is out of numerical sequence. But they should be, I hope, Mr. President, Your Honours, in the order in which they will be reviewed with this witness. So with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, you are allowed to ask some leading questions in the hope that we could get through the events of 1992 and come directly to the events in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. I will say -- I should tell the Chamber in candour, we will spend -- or I had proposed that we will spend a fair amount of time on the second half of 1992, because, as you've heard from other witnesses, this is the full story of the expanding -- ever-expanding takeover by the HVO authority in Mostar. I will try to take it quickly, but there is a substantial amount of ground to cover in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this witness is not the first witness we've heard about the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope you will bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct. And perhaps it will assist the Chamber if -- Mr. President, if I tell you this may be about the last. So after today, maybe I can announce that we will be into -- primarily into a different category of witnesses from this day forward, for the most part, obviously with some exceptions. But we are going to be -- this will be one of the Chamber's, respectfully, last opportunities to hear from a broader overview witness on these developments. I do appreciate the fact that the Chamber has heard this before. This witness brings a unique perspective to it because of his high position in the Islamic church and his very close involvement in these events. But I understand, Mr. President, your concerns, and again I will tell the Chamber now - I'm making it very open to the Defence as well - this will be about the last witness that the Prosecution will call in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, if you can look, please, a bundle of exhibits have been put in front of you. Now, you will know already - and everyone in the courtroom will see, of course - they are English translations usually on top, followed by the B/C/S, or Serbo-Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in many instances, Judge Diarra - but I can't say, unfortunately, all - but in many instances there is also a French translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to Exhibit P125.1, and just -- if you can just familiarise yourself by looking at that document for a moment. Is that a copy of the decision dated the 29th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Taking the President's cue, if I'm allowed, let me take you straight to an issue in the case, and then we can talk about particular parts or sentences of the document itself. Let me take you straight to it, if I'm allowed. There has been some suggestion, Mr. Smajkic, that by this document, the HDZ, the Bosnian-Croat political party, the HDZ, or the HVO was essentially given the right to take over Mostar. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. The Croatian Defence Council only received this armed part, that is, the defence aspect of the defence of Mostar, and the Municipal Crisis Staff remained a civil authority. However, the HVO took this as an excuse to grab power, in other words, to proclaim a war of government of Mostar and basically carry out a Putsch against civilian authorities and take over control, both in civilian and military aspects. Also, the possibility was opened for the Ministry of Internal Affairs, as one segment of the defence forces, to play a role, and also to the Territorial Defence, which was composed exclusively of Bosnia forces. They were allowed to exist. In addition, in one of the points --

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness did not respond to the Prosecutor's question but is taking it further and is making conclusions about what some people may have thought and agreed, so I propose to have it stricken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I also object but on different grounds. My objection is that this is a religious official. This is not a politician, and he is not an expert in this. I think that he should be disallowed from giving answers to questions that relate to policies and politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think everybody has his view and his opinions towards policy issues, no matter what his occupation is. So in this way, this question is allowed. But there's a problem in the answering of this question; that is, Witness, you have to answer the questions straight to the question asked by the Prosecutor and do not elaborate unless it is really necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I appreciate the Court's guidance. In fairness to the witness, I must say the question was -- I put a central issue in the case to him. My question was: Is that true? And his response was, "That is not correct." So I think it was directly responsive. He directly answered my question. It is true that he did go on, then, to give the reasons for his answer. But I will continue to take him through some additional specific points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Smajkic, for instance, if I can direct your attention -- what I would like to do is we can just go through this document, which might also serve to provide some structure to your testimony. If I can direct your attention, please, to the bottom of the first page -- well, I can't say in B/C/S. It's under roman numeral II, if you can find that. There's a reference in that first paragraph under -- I guess there is only one paragraph, which is roman numeral II -- to, for instance, the members of the Ministry of the Interior. Now, up until the time that this document was signed, was that a multi-ethnic police force?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after this document was signed, what happened to that police force? What happened to it after this document?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: After the HVO took over power, it changed the command structure of the police. People who were loyal to the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna were left in their posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the next section, roman numeral III, it makes the statement: "The Croatian Defence Council consists of members of the Muslim and Croatian peoples." And would you tell the Chamber, please, were there any Muslim members in the higher -- if I can put it this way -- the higher leadership positions of the Croatian Defence Council? Were there any Muslim members at that level?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: No, that was not the case. In -- there were no Muslims in senior command positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your direction to paragraph roman numeral IV, the first part, it says: "The upper composition of the commanding corps of the Croatian Defence Council shall mirror the ethnic composition of active-duty soldiers." Did that happen? Was the commanding officer corps of the HVO, did it reflect the ethnic makeup of the rank and file of the multi-ethnic HVO?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: No. These were members -- that is, the officers were from the Croatian side, at least senior ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In reference, in the interest of efficiency, taking the President's words into mind, in terms of roman numeral V and VI, in reference to law enforcement in the judicial authorities, the end of paragragh roman numeral VI says: "The ethnic structure of these institutions shall reflect the ethnic structure of active-duty soldiers." Can you again tell us, was that true or was that, in fact, followed, law enforcement and judicial structures reflected the ethnic makeup of the community?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Not at all. It did not reflect it. It is mentioned in the documents that the representation should be proportionate. However, when the HVO took over power, they established military police, and the military police marginalised the authority of the civilian police. And the Minister of the Interior, which they had appointed, fired all the Muslims within the police structure so that the individuals who did not recognise the Croatian authority and failed to give an oath were sacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me, in a similar fashion, direct your attention to roman numeral VII and IX, and I'll further assist you in this way, again, in the interest of efficiency. There are references in both of those paragraphs to recognition or that due regard be given to the legal organs of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you please describe to the Chamber what you observed around this time and thereafter of the HVO's attitude toward the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: This government simply ignored all the institutions of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It completely stifled the work of the Crisis Staff and replaced all the structures of the civilian authority, which was in direct opposition to all the legal provisions of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Crisis Staff was supposed to -- that is -- was supposed to establish an executive council of the city government in order to allow these institutions to operate, but the HVO completely obstructed that and took over so that Milivoje Gagro, who had been a legally elected officer of that government, he resigned in protest for not being able to discharge his duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to remind the Chamber, Mr. Gagro, himself, was a Croat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we move on, in your answer just now, you started out by saying, "This government simply ignored all the institutions of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." When you said "this government," which government were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the war government of the city of Mostar, which was presided by Mr. Jadranko Topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which political party or organisation was he a part of?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That was the HDZ, or the Croatian Democratic Union Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time, in fact, around this time, after the April 29th agreement, that you were asked to go to Split in Croatia and make some sort of appearance on Croatian TV?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please just tell the Chamber about that? I'm going to invite you to give just your own words, a narrative account, although please do keep it somewhat concise, if you will.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I was asked to appear on television in Split with a delegation made of one Bosniak politician and one religious leader and, on the other side, a Croat politician and a representative of the Catholic community. On the set day, we came to the TV studio in Split, and were met with ovations. I didn't understand immediately what was going on, but they were coming to Topic, Mr. Topic, and congratulating him on his office of the mayor of the city of Mostar. His brother, Marin, who was with him, said that at long last, the Croats have acquired their capital. And in a direct question the host of the programme asked of Mr. Topic who was the president to Bosnia-Herzegovina, to his mind; that is, whom he recognised as the president. He stated publicly that that was Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you come to understand your role there, having now told us what you just said - why did they want you - to the extent you can tell us, based on what you saw and heard, your role to be there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question on the grounds it calls for pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, I'm not asking you to get into anyone else's head, but you were invited -- who invited you to go to Split?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: People from the Croat Defence Council. And it was the president of the then SDA, Ismet Hadziosmanovic, was the one who selected me and another person. He sent Hadziosmanovic, and asked that the two of us, Salahovic -- and asked that the two of us represent the Islamic community. At that meeting, it was said that Camil Salahovic would address political issues, that I should not do that, and that it was up to me to call for humanitarian assistance, to launch an appeal for the humanitarian aid to Mostar, which had already been shelled and thoroughly ruined by that time, and to -- so that the cameras could show that the Muslims, that is, Bosniaks and Croats, represented one front. We were to go there and act and impersonate something, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am again objecting to this last part of the witness's answer, because he's again giving us his opinion about what other people thought, and I do not think that the witnesses should not testify in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me briefly respond, please. I'm not asking -- and if the witness is misinterpreting my questions or if my questions are not correctly put, that's my fault and I apologise. I think the witness, however, can say what he observed and what he came to expect and what he saw going on around him, what he saw and observed, can make his own conclusions and share those with the Chamber as to what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I'm not objecting to questions -- to the question. The question as a question was all right, but in his -- in towards the end of his answer, the witness began to tell us about what he thought that somebody else had thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so. I think the witness answered the question perfectly. At least we know that what his role was at that television interview, and we are interested to hear that. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me come back to what you were just -- where you just took us, to this: When you were asked to go to Split and appear on Croatian TV, were you asked or told to wear your full - forgive me again if I use the wrong terminology - but your religious wear? As a Mufti, did you come dressed in clerical clothing?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did anyone tell you anything more about what they expected that they wanted you to say or what they expected to say during this TV broadcast?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Not in Mostar, but when we arrived at that TV station, they expected our side to lend support to that option; that is, to Mate Boban's option.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were there, did any of the other representatives, Mr. Topic or others, did they make any -- was there any conversation about the Neretva River?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation, but I understood your question in English. When the programme host asked Mr. Topic what was the ultimate goal, what were the boundaries of the city of Mostar, he said that it would be the Neretva River, which means that the city of Mostar, that is, according to the then option of the Croat politicians, was to be divided into a Croat and a Serb part. I am not a politician, Your Honours, but then this politician who was to speak on behalf of the Muslim party asked, begged, went down on his knees before Mr. Topic, to say that the HVO's goal was the liberation of the whole territory of the city of Mostar, rather than to go only as far as the Neretva River, which divides the city into two. I remember very well indeed that he said that he dared not go back to Mostar or face the Bosniak people unless Topic withdrew that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you continue, please, let's have for the record, if you can assist us, what was the name of this other Bosniak or Muslim representative who was making these requests to Mr. Topic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Salahovic, Camil Salahovic, called "Limi," a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you present when Mr. Topic made any response to Mr. Salahovic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I'm not getting any interpretation. Yes, that's fine now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies, and please let us know if you have any problems. My question to you was: Were you present when Mr. Topic made any response to Mr. Salahovic, if -- when he raised these questions or concerns that you were telling us about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I was present. That television then cut short the programme and a very embittered discussion about that, Topic's statement, ensued. But he did not deny, he did not withdraw what he had said for the television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we are moving forward a bit. Did you learn about this time that in fact there had been some agreement between the Croats and Serbs about boundaries in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Needless to say, it all seemed to indicate that there had been a previous agreement between the Serbs and the Croats on the division of Herzegovina, and one could see it on the ground as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, and the Chamber's attention, next to Exhibit 126.1 in everyone's packet of materials; including, Mr. Smajkic, the one before you. I'll have to tell you this document is only in English and was prepared, at least the parts that I've seen, in English.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Chamber will have seen this before. If I can have the assistance of interpretation, please, if I can have the second page of this exhibit, going to paragraphs numbered 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since it's not in B/C/S in front of you, sir, let me read that to you, and if you listen to interpretation, I'll ask you a couple of questions about this. "Number 1: In the city of Mostar, the Serbian side considers the Neretva River to be the border line, while the Croatian side considers the entire city of Mostar to be within the Croatian constituent unit. "Number 2: South of Mostar, the Croatian side considers the entire area delineated in 1939, in other words, the borders of the Hrvatska Banovina, to be within the Croatian constituent unit. The Serbian side considers the Neretva River to be the border line between the Croatian and the Serbian constituent units." I don't think, actually, on reflection, we need paragraph 3. Let me, however, direct, if I can, everyone's attention to paragraph 6. "In view of the agreement --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, I've been cautioned to slow down. Forgive me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "In view of the agreement outlined above, no more reasons obtain for an armed conflict between the Croatians and Serbs in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." This document prepared as of May 6, 1992, at 2400 hours, over the names of Radovan Karadzic and Mate Boban. My question to you, sir, based on that, what was just read to you: Are you familiar with that, and do you remember hearing about these developments around this time in May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I did not have this document before me ever. Yes, this is an agreement between Karadzic and Boban - I know about that - and I'm aware that such a meeting took place, but I was not familiar with the exact wording. However, the developments on the ground were in full correspondence with this document, in full agreement with this document. I do know that -- well, it is possible that the relations between the Serbs and Croats fluctuated, that in the beginning, the border line was at the Neretva. Then perhaps they started thinking about the exchange of territories and that border line was shifted to the boundaries of the Banovina. That is true. But in my communication with the armed forces of Serbia, in the Neretva valley, during the aggression, that is, still I saw heated resistance, fierce resistance, being put up to this document, because of the retreat from the valley. They blamed -- that they cursed Karadzic and all the other Serb leaders, that they had to withdraw without offering strong resistance, that they had to withdraw, that is, from the Neretva Valley and Mostar, without any resistance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, let me just ask you a couple of items about this, and then we will finish with this document. You mentioned just now -- sorry, I want to be exact. You mentioned just now the reference to the boundaries of the Banovina. What did you know or understand that to be, what reference is that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That was a product of the former Croatia, that is, Croatia in the times of World War II or, rather, we can say Pavelic's state. Or let me try to put it even more clearly. It wasn't by accident that I said the HVO at times acted some offensives or something, but in point of fact, they did not want to conquer territories after they had reached the boundaries of the Banovina, so that the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if they wanted to advance, they could have done that. However, the Croat Defence Council, which was a partner at the time, refused to move an inch beyond the boundary of the Banovina, which is very convincing proof. And I knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to a part of the witness's answer. The witness shows us his knowledge of history. All of a sudden, he starts testifying as a historian about the historical circumstances, and his account is completely inaccurate, at least insofar as the Banovinas are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, on the one hand, the witness is giving his view on those events which might touch upon some historical background. On the other hand, Mr. Scott, we have been spent almost an hour on these background issues, and we haven't realised whether all this event is related to the relevant parts of the indictment. You didn't mention the accused's name, Mr. Naletilic, Tuta. We are to hear the direct evidence concerning the accused persons, not to hear all the background issues around Mostar. We know that is very necessary for us to have some background information about that time. But too much information will just get us lost, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. I'm in the position of not being able to completely agree with Your Honour. We are required to prove -- the Prosecution is required to prove, among other things, that the conduct that these accused participated in was part of a widespread and systematic campaign, that it was part of a widespread and systematic plan, resulting or based upon persecution on religious, political, ethnic and national grounds; that they were not acting individually; that they were not acting on a lark on their own, simply on a personal matter. This was part and parcel of a plan, of a scheme that was hatched by the HDZ and the HVO and supported by the Croatian government that goes back to 1992 and earlier. We are required to prove that. Now, we have asked throughout these Pre-Trial proceedings -- and I understand that the Chamber, of course, unfortunately, was not a party, was not even constituted at the time of the Pre-Trial proceedings. During that time, I think the time has come -- I think the time has come -- I see Mr. Seric on his feet. I will finish what I have to say, please, first, and then Mr. Seric can respond. Through that time, we asked counsel for both accused to agree to certain things. We tendered to them a number of times potential agreed statement of facts, including these very facts, and they refused. They put everything in issue. They have never agreed to anything to streamline this case. They have required us to prove everything. Even in the short time before the trial started, I once again sent letters to them asking them to stipulate to as many as 150 -- some 150 background facts, and they refused to do so. Now, you can say that's their right. But if that's their position, Your Honour, then the Prosecution has no opportunity -- has no alternative but to prove its case. And we're trying to do that as efficiently as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I couldn't agree with you more. As far as this witness, I wish to say that the Prosecutor is trying to use this witness -- within the presumed historical context, he is trying to establish a link between my clients and a product which emerged during World War II, and I do not think that this witness can be asked to testify about things that happened then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, we believe that it is essential for us to hear this witness, but we just want you to do it as efficient as possible and as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I do appreciate that. If the Chamber will allow me on some matters, I will -- as you invited me, in fact, to do a few minutes, I will try to lead and to be more efficient through these matters. But of course, if I do so, I can expect, I suppose at some point, to draw objection, and I'll be in the Chamber's hands as to how you would like me to proceed. But I will do the best I can, of course. Finishing I think, Mr. President, about two additional questions on this document, and then we can move forward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you heard of these developments around this time, which we are told here about a meeting between Karadzic and Boban in the city of Graz, Austria, did it ever come to your attention what was the position, if you know, of the Bosniak community, whether any representatives of the Bosnians, the Bosniaks, were invited to attend these negotiations to draw the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: No, no Bosniaks were not represented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was -- my final question on this -- and what was, if you know, the response of the Bosniak community in Mostar where you were a senior religious leader when you heard about this plan or document to divide up Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The Bosniak people was against any division of Bosnia, rather the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because that year, as an autonomous and sovereign country, Bosnia had been recognised by the United Nations and even by Croatia itself. And with the permission of the Honourable Court, I should like to say, how did I get involved in these political waters, even though that is not my job? And that is also in answer to your question. Because people, Bosniaks, came to me. They came to me. From the very beginning, they disagreed with turning the power over to the HVO, and they saw it, in a way, as a betrayal on the part of the then Bosniak leadership, because that leadership kept -- said nothing. They were just -- and did not take any steps, did not do anything in order to offset such activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, I want to have you look briefly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If you would come to your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Taking the President's remarks to heart, I want you to look briefly at Exhibit 157.1, 162.1, and 162.2, which will be the next three documents in everyone's bundle. Do you recognise each of those three documents as either documents that you were involved in preparing or were familiar with at this time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was an active participant in all these three instances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And briefly, if you take those documents together, can you just briefly say why -- what was the nature of these publications or correspondence, the first dated the 10th of July, 1992; the second dated the 8th of August, 1992; the third dated the 9th of August, 1992? What was this all about? What were these documents -- why did they come about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and what were they trying to address?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm doing this, Mr. President, because I could spend a substantial amount of time on each document, but I'm going to try not to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were these documents about, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: These documents reflect the wish of all Bosniak institutions, military, civilian, political, and others, to regulate their relations with the Croats because they did not follow the preconceived course from the very beginning. We tried to strike a balance in the political presentation, in the authorities, in the army, an equitable treatment of the language, an equitable distribution of offices in companies which still worked and to which people were assigned pursuant to HVO decrees. So a possible gentlemen's agreement that would be translated into life, to remove, that is, all possible troubles, those roughnesses which had already begun to burn our communication in everyday life. We started to have this Croat component, which was the dominating one; and the Bosniak side, which was always the client, the plaintiff, always begging for something, begging not to destroy Mostar, and also begging for the liberation of the territory without armed forces. We realised that they did not want that. In life, I saw it with my own eyes. When they would reach a territory which we could take, then the Croat component refused to join us and move ahead. So from joint symbols and emblems in the army and everywhere, everywhere. So they kept keeping alive certain problems, certain difficulties which made our relations very difficult. In all these documents, we were requesting to establish our joint position towards the war, towards the common enemy, towards criminals and war criminals, to protect vigorously all the values, religious, cultural, tradition of all the peoples, and so on and so forth. So this is basically the framework.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm going to cut you off for the moment. I see it's 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a couple of additional questions about these particular documents, and then we will move on after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for your information, my client needed to be taken to see a physician urgently because he did not feel -- had any feelings on his left side, including his head, this morning, but he only reported this to me during the break. He was just taken away -- I think we can move on, and this is my client's wish also, but I have a different request. Can we only work until 1.00 today, because I would like to go and visit him in the detention unit in the afternoon, and I hope that you can grant me this request. We would go back to the regular schedule tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we are sorry to hear that your client is not feeling well. I hope he could see a doctor as soon as possible. And I'm also glad that you allowed us to proceed this morning without the presence of your client. And as for the afternoon's sitting, I think we should get the report from doctor first and to see whether your client is suitable to sit for this afternoon's session. So during the lunch break, we will await the report from you or from the detention unit about conditions of your client. Then we'll make the decisions - maybe not in the court - and we will inform you as soon as we have made that decision. Is that all right, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Scott, are you ready to call your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are ready to start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, in terms of the three documents that were placed before you before the break, I'm just going to have - well, of course, depending on your answers, of course - two or three questions on each document, and I'll ask you to please respond as directly to my questions as you reasonably can. Referring to Exhibit P157.1, do you recall whether this document, among others perhaps, was sent to Jadranko Topic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I cannot find the document. What document is it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 157.1. It has the title, "The Basic Arrangements of Current Political Relations Between the Croats and Muslims."

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm not suggesting -- so my question is clear, I'm not suggesting that the document itself is addressed to -- in a "Dear Mr. Topic" sort of way, but do you know whether this document, among others, was provided to Mr. Topic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I know that with certainty, because the first signature to the left is Mr. Izet Hadziosmanovic, president of the SDA. This was the political party which was in partnership with the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And perhaps I should say in that regard, directing your attention to the last page of that document itself, of course in the B/C/S version, among others, does it bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I -- if you can assist us, under roman numeral II, under the heading -- small heading (b), and the second bullet item, if I can say that, it makes the statement: "We demand that all the fighters, both Muslim and Croat, have equal status."

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Bosniak community believe at that time, as of July 1992, that in fact the Muslims and Croat components of the armed forces were being treated equally?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: No, that equal status never existed at no time. This is why these documents were drafted, as they followed the events on the ground. We had support, but it was only in words. However, in reality, the facts were the exact opposite of what the agreement was; in fact, the one that the HVO had nominally agreed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to roman numeral III, and just with reference to the police force, was the situation similar there? To state the contrary -- if I can put it, to state the contrary of the request being -- or the observation being made here, was it the fact that there was not equal and proportional participation of Muslims and Croats in the police forces?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Correct. That is exactly right, in essence, in short.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to the -- under roman numeral IV, second sentence, second paragraph or sentence, it says this: "The symbols of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be introduced on all official signs and seals." Will you please tell the Chamber briefly, what was the situation at that time in terms of the governmental signs and seals that were being displayed in the Mostar region?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: In the documents that were issued by the HVO institutions, you could find no sign or symbol that would intimate the existence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the contrary, there were Croatian symbols and stamps, and everything that was in direct opposition to the constitution and legal principles on which Bosnia and Herzegovina had been established. We can say -- we can say that those arrangements, the arrangements that regulated the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, were modelled after those of the Republic of Croatia. And this is why this document was drafted, because people could not accept to fight under such symbols, because it would turn out that the Croats were the ones who liberated the territory and that Bosniaks were never to be found. And this was precisely the behaviour of the Croatian officials at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, I'm going to move on. Of course, if the Chamber has additional questions of these documents, they will -- the Judges will have an opportunity to put questions to you, you understand, at the end of your testimony. Moving to the Exhibit P162.1, which is the next document in your bundle, I think only -- well, a couple of questions. Looking to the -- well, strike that. Can you tell us briefly how this document was prepared and who signed it -- not signed this document, but tell us about that. I think you can shed some light on this.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: This is the document of 8 August 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: This is a document which expresses a desire of the Bosniak people in which the Bosniaks take position to the important issues at that time, the war, the illegal institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the law and -- the laws and customs of war and the way individuals are handled and their rights of all people who exist in that territory that were under our control; in other words, how we saw that these arrangements should be made on all these issues. I did not sign this copy, but this resolution was drafted by a group of intellectuals of Mostar, and they signed it. 152 Bosniak intellectuals signed it, and it was distributed in the streets of Mostar, Konjic, and Jablanica. More than 10.000 signatures were collected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to Roman Numeral I, the fourth paragraph under Roman Numeral I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll give you a chance to find that, counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It states -- that paragraph or sentence states: "The Muslims advocate the integral and indivisible state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and do not recognise any para-Statal - I'm not sure about that word - para-State creations." Was that, in fact, the position of the Bosniak community at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Completely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to Exhibit 162.2 which again will be the next document, this document appears to raise some concerns or issues about the movement of Bosniak or Muslim refugees to areas outside or beyond Mostar, just to set the scene, if you will, for that document. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: This was the reception of refugees who escaped from the areas controlled by the Serbs. After the Serbs had pulled out of Mostar, these people found refuge in the Mostar area. They were mostly from Nevesinje, Gacko, which are now in Republic of Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, at least my screen has stopped after the answer "completely so." I don't know if it's just this table or everybody's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please check it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Counsel is correct. I don't see it either. Shall we try again? Is it coming?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apology, Mr. Smajkic. I'll try to restate my question. I just asked you to turn to Exhibit 162.2, and it appears that none of that was, in fact, caught on the record. This is a document that appears to discuss an issue about the further evacuation or displacement of Muslim or Bosniak refugees that were coming to the Mostar area at that time. Can you briefly, briefly, please, tell the Chamber about what that problem was and what was happening?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It happened that when people who had been expelled by the Serbs, people from Eastern Herzegovina found refuge in Mostar. And I was personally involved and our community was involved in receiving these refugees. However, the Croatian side did not wish these people to remain in Mostar. Instead, they prepared not buses but trucks, which were to transfer these persons to Zenica where, in their opinion, Muslims were to live and reside. Of course, we firmly resisted that. And for a period of time, we prevented it. On the other side - and I want to make this clear to the Chamber - they were very glad to receive Croats from other areas in Mostar. So in parallel, the city was being emptied of Muslims and filled with Croats from other areas, if I can put it that way, and that was all part of the plan that I think we will address next. This document is a demarche of sorts, and those who had -- this was to also warn that this deportation of Bosniaks was not going to be ignored.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just to move on, finally question on this document, then: The point of it, as you said, is that by contrast, Croat refugees who were coming to Mostar during this time were not being forced out of Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: No, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move on. We are not looking at those documents now, but this Mr. Gagro, who had been the elected Croat head of the Crisis Staff, did he continue for some time to make efforts to hold the Crisis Staff, if you will, together as the legitimate government body?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: For about a month. Since that -- the beginning -- since the 29th of April until the end of May. After that, his role was reduced to nil, and he resigned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who reduced his role to nil?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the -- can you answer this question: When the HVO or the HDZ took power in Mostar, did they work through the existing government institutions of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or did they establish separate institutions?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: They established separate institutions, so that we had separate police, all the institutions, completely separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Boban, the Chamber I'm sure knows by now, was the president of Herceg-Bosna. Can you tell the Chamber, was there ever a democratic election where the Bosniaks voted for Mr. Boban as the president of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: No, never. And just as over there, that is, they had made a Putsch, a coup d'etat, in the authorities in Mostar, and that is their problem, which, however, was our concern, within the entity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they did the same thing, removed the lawful elected Mr. Kljuic; after that, Mr. Brkic; until they eventually elected the individual who was to carry out the plan agreed in Graz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, I'm going to cut you off a bit there so we can go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to follow your direction at this point and ask some leading questions, and, again, I'll be in the Chamber's hands as to counsel's position on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that during this time, and as a result of the HVO takeover in Mostar, the post office in Mostar was renamed the "Croatian Post Office"? I'm not looking at documents now, sir. If you could just answer my question.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The post office wasn't the only one. Every single institution in the town was given the prefix of "Croatia." We had the Croat water supply. We had the Croat post office. Every enterprise, every company, had the word "Croat."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what happened in terms of the public schools in Mostar, in terms of the curriculum and language in the schools?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: In schools, likewise, they immediately began to implement the Croatian curriculum. The university was renamed. It was -- used to be called Dzemal Bijedic, and it was renamed the Croat University in Mostar. The new steering board was elected with Croat membership, or rather, one or two Bosniaks whom they perceived as loyal to them. And you have a document here that the Croat language -- Croatian language was introduced into schools, which we refused. In other words, a complete supremacy of Croats took place, and the Bosniaks were pushed to the margins, or rather, none of their cultural, religious, or any other rights were recognised any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we come to the next document, let me ask you this: Did you ever have meetings or conversations with Mr. Topic and another HVO leader named Jadranko Prlic, P-r-l-i-c, about the issue of language and the schools, and if so, just briefly tell the Chamber about that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I shall be very brief. In the beginning of 1993, that is, during the mid-term recess, mid-term holidays, we had a meeting with Mr. Prlic and a team of his. They came to the then offices of the SDA in order to discuss the issue of the language in school, that is, the name of the language, because both the school IDs and the certificates already said that our children were learning the Croatian language. And our teachers boycotted the instruction and were refusing to come back to school for the second term of the 1992-93 school year. They went on strike, and children too refused to go to school. So Prlic came then to discuss the matter. They asked me to be present there -- I mean the Bosniaks asked me to be present there, simply because they wanted -- they trusted me fully because some other SDA politicians -- because they had lost trust in some other SDA politicians who had participated in negotiations before that, as they were constantly making concessions to the Croats. On that occasion, Mr. Prlic denied the existence of the Bosniak language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I didn't mean to interrupt you, but I thought perhaps you were going on on some things more than we needed. But at the end of your answer just now you said as a result of this meeting or at the meeting, Mr. Prlic denied the existence of the Bosnian language. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think Mr. Prlic -- I'm sorry, I think Mr. Prlic may be a name that the Chamber has not heard so much about. Can you describe to the Chamber who Jadranko Prlic was?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: He was the Prime Minister of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, the highest executive in the government, one of the most influential people in the Croat Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move ahead to the exhibit -- the next document in your packet, Exhibit Z -- I'm sorry, it was an old habit. Not Z. P168.1. Can you tell the Chamber what that is, please, first of all?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: You mean this addressed to the Croat Democratic Union? I can't find the numbers that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. It should be the one right before that. There is something that looks like a report card, if I can call it that.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what that is?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the document that I mentioned where one can see very clearly this is a school year 1991-92, and a lad, a Bosniak, attending an electrical school, and you can see here the subjects in which he received instruction, and the first subject here is Croatian language. And you can also see that there is -- that the background of this is the -- this seal, that is. The chequer-board, the Croatian one, you can see it very well here. This is the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, let me just break up your answers in little smaller pieces, if we can; sometimes I think it's easier for everyone in the courtroom. You just now referred to a symbol or a sign, and I want to give everyone a chance to see that. Looking -- are you talking about on the middle of the page, a document --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... behind, if you will, the text that's on, if you would, the stationery? Is that what you're referring to? The checkerboard?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a Croatian symbol?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Croatian symbol, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the top of this page the words -- and I won't try to say it --, well, Hrvatska Herceg-Bosna -- that is, the Croatian Community --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it say anything -- you can tell by the name of this person, can you, that this is a Muslim student or Bosniak student?
