utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I know that -- I know him personally. I know the family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is there anywhere on the report card, if you will, that's indicated he was studying or graded on the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just so the record is clear for the Chamber, when you say the Croatian language is referenced, that is the first item in the box, Hrvatska?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: And if I may add, this document was printed in Grude. As you can see, this is early 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You're referring to the stationery information on the lower left corner? All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's right yes; that is, the document was prepared in the early days of '92; that is, since the Croat community was set up in November '91. So evidently they were keeping pace with the organisation of this para-State and documents were being prepared to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see the date here down in that lower left corner, it looks to be "1/92," which I suppose we would take as January '92.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the Chamber can draw its own conclusions about the sequence of events on that. Mr. Smajkic, I want to move on in the interests of time, please. I think you have touched on a wide range of topics. Of course, the Chamber can follow with its own questions. Let me jump to the topic of the Muslim members or the Bosniak members of the HVO during this time. Can you tell the Chamber, or, again, if counsel will allow, is it true that the Bosniak community proposed and, in fact, designed a common insignia, a patch or an insignia, that would be worn by both Croatian and Bosniak soldiers that would be neutral and a common insignia to each of them? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I know about it very well. Because I saw personally the proposals and the designs. But only the Bosniak side was ready to have on one -- to have -- to include in one emblem, either on the sleeve or wherever, to have it with both the symbol of the lily and the symbol of the HVO. However, the military of the HVO -- rather, the Croat component never agreed to that. And this continued to be a bone of contention throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the record is clear, there was a patch, in fact, that was designed and made, manufactured, of a lily, which is typically a symbol of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And when you say the HVO symbol, are you referring to, for instance, a chequer-board pattern?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was a patch, an actual patch, that had both symbols on it? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Muslim soldiers actually wearing that patch?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I did, yes. When those emblems were promoted, yes, quite a number of people began to wear them, and they did so for a while. However, the Croat side did not agree to that, and so it came to an end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If we can go on to the next document. I'm going to, again, skip over a number of items. Exhibit P173.1, which, again, should be the next one in your bundle, would you just look at that document for a moment and tell us, are you familiar with that document?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: And the date of the document is?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 14th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will tell the Chamber that after this document, there's only one other document in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this another in these continuing series of communications from the Bosniak community, if I can say, stating various grievances that the community held at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Quite. In one passage, it says to remove and overcome a series of systemic errors committed by the HVO regarding the relations between the Croats and the Bosniaks. But you have the document before you. I do not really want to comment on it. In this document, you can see a whole string of facts. However, the significance rests with the fact this was signed by the president of the regional board of the SDA, Ismet Hadziosmanovic, because he was one of the Bosniaks whom the Croat side recognised. If he signed this document, he confirms all the other documents in which he also participated; that is, it corroborates all the statements about the degradation, the humiliation of the Bosniak component, both the civilian and the military one, in the -- in all the earlier joint efforts to defend the country. There is one item, if you like - it is very important - that the HVO prohibited the work of Radio Mostar and called it, as we have already said, a Croat station. It became the Croat Radio Mostar, with a Croat staff, and they were to inform the public and channel the -- streamline the information of the public in the direction they preferred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, let me just ask you two questions before concluding with this document: Just to tie this into your testimony just a few moments ago, if I can ask you to look -- unfortunately, there aren't paragraph headings on this, so it's a bit more difficult. But about halfway through the document -- probably less than halfway. It would be -- I'm sorry, number 2. Forgive me. If I can direct you to paragraph numbered 2 out of approximately -- looks like there's 15 altogether. If you look at number 2, is that again, a reference to the efforts by the Bosniak community to have a common insignia that you were telling us about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, one of these items refers to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In reference to paragraph number 6, what was happening to the property of Bosniak refugees when they were being sent on to the Republic of Croatia or elsewhere? What happened to their property?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: In Grude, all the property, notably cars and valuables which the Bosniak refugees had, was seized. Moreover, the humanitarian aid arriving through that territory did not reach any Bosniak destination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any fundamental changes come about as a result of this letter by Mr. Hadziosmanovic? That is, were any of these grievances addressed to the satisfaction of the Bosniak community?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Nothing changed at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me for asking one question that I missed, because it directly relates to, of course, your role. In paragraph 15, it talks about the restriction on the movement of clerics. Can you tell us what was happening in that regard at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The HVO police, when they manned all the checkpoints and controlled all the entrances and exits from the town, refused to allow anyone to exit the city without proper authorization. And at that time, we still had those territories in the municipalities of Capljina and Stolac outside of Mostar where we had to go for funerals, for some religious activities. So our Imans had to go there and come back, and they could not get passes. So we asked -- we told Mr. Hadziosmanovic, our political representative, about this. He knew that. I had forgotten about it because there are a number of things here. He included that in his document, because we wanted him to resolve it with the HDZ and HVO to avoid further complications, because they were happening time and time again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, let me ask you to turn next to Exhibit P190. Again, it should be the next document. I think only about two questions. Well, other than the fact, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, is it addressed to you on the first page, to Mufti Seid Smajkic, personally?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It is. It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall - and if so, can you describe to the Chamber - the circumstances in which Mr. Jadranko -- or Jadran Topic sent this letter to you on the 11th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Topic, as the representative of the authority at that time, to find some office space for me, because at that time, I worked in the west part of the town of Mostar in very simple offices -- rather, in student's hostel, which accommodated refugees from Nevesinje, Podvelezje, and some other places. And he didn't really heed much to this request that I had made, but he, nevertheless, did his best to find excellent accommodation for my colleague, Bishop Peric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can stop you there for this purpose: Directing your attention to the second paragraph of Mr. Topic's letter, did that accurately summarise essentially the HVO position at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Topic accorded the building of the great men of Bosnia and the mayor of Mostar, Mujaga Komadinar, and allotted it to the bishop. I objected, and I call that decision whereby he allotted that area, that building, to the bishop, I said that it was an unlawful decision because he did not represent the lawful authority of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Had he been my mayor -- if he were my mayor, too, he would also take to accommodate me properly. And this letter and this threat ensued then and that I was meddling in politics and I should steer clear of that and mind my own business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that answer. Let me go back so the record is clear specifically on the question of paragraph 2, starting the words "The Croatian Defence Council ..." Given what you've told us today, does that paragraph summarise the position of the HVO at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And directing your attention to several paragraphs below that, where the paragraph starts with the words "We are sorry to see ..." and going to the end of that paragraph, is that what you are referring to just now when you say that essentially Mr. Topic said -- well, to use the vernacular -- "butt out"?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the episode that I refer to. I considered the decision unlawful, and I sent a letter of protest saying that I was very happy that he had found where to accommodate the bishop. But he told me personally "I cannot sleep" -- these are his words. "I cannot sleep because my bishop is arriving tomorrow." And I said, I went when the bishop was ordained. I was present at his inauguration, and he should get his premises, but I should get them, too. And then he told me, well, that depends on you, which I suppose meant that I should be cooperative, that I should be humble, and renounce the interests of the Bosniak people and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's continue on, please. Mr. Smajkic, I'm only going to ask you this question just to remind the Chamber of another event during this period of time: Was it during late 1992 approximately that, among other things, a man name Zihad Demirovic was made the regional president of the SDA in place of Mr. Hadziosmanovic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Zijad, which is Z-i-j-a-d.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My mistake. Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: He became the president of the regional SDA for Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move forward to January 1993. Can you tell the Chamber, were certain ultimatums stated by the HVO in January 1993, and if so, please tell the Chamber what those ultimatums were.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: There were constantly some ultimatums. But in a nutshell, we had -- I should say the Bosniak people, and the Bosniak population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were given a deadline of the 20th of January to place themselves under the command of Croatian Defence Council; otherwise, they would be disarmed and driven out to the territories that they considered to be Bosniak in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Smajkic, I'm going to attempt to do this quite quickly, if you'll work with me on this. I want you to look at Exhibits P214 and P215 next in your bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, the first is a decision by Jadranko Prlic dated the 15th of January, 1993. The second document is an order by the Herceg-Bosna Minister of Defence, Bruno Stojic, also dated the 15th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, what I want to do is ask you, if you look at those documents briefly, those two, of course in the B/C/S version, does what is stated in those documents comport with what you knew was happening on the ground in mid-January 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I did not review these documents, but there was great anxiety on the part of Bosniaks during that period. They asked us that we express a common will in a meeting, in a joint meeting, because it was -- for us, it was a matter of survival at that point, and it was seen that the HVO might make good on their threats. This is why we assembled and drafted certain documents and sent them out to all the relevant parties so that these threats would be dealt with, because we could sense that the situation was verging on being out of control, escalating, and this is why I say I did not see these documents. But the persons who were in politics and who were in the units of the BH army corps had such information, and we drafted a document -- I think it was on the 17th of January. There was -- that was a period of general tension, and our efforts were channelled towards trying to prevent the escalation of this conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me, just to point your attention to a couple of things before going on to your documents. On P214, which is the decision by Jadranko Prlic, paragraph number 5 says the decision shall be implemented in five days starting from today, 15 of January, 1993. Just keep that in mind, if you will, for a moment. If you go to Mr. Stojic's order of the same date, paragraph number 7, that says, the deadline for carrying out this order is 1900 hours on the 20th of January, 1993. So my question to you is: Did the Bosniak community or the leadership at that time know that, essentially, the ultimatum was that if certain things didn't happen by the 20th of January, some action would follow?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That is why we had gathered. This was simply the reason for us getting together, so that we could prepare the document which followed. The Bosniaks indeed believed that our partners, so far that is, were very serious in their intentions and that they simply wanted to drive out the forces who would not fight or subordinate themselves to them, even though these young men of ours were born there and their identity and their existence was being put in question. And because of these threats, we gathered at a great assembly and we took all this very seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before going to those documents, you said just now in your answer -- you said "our partners," and perhaps everyone in the courtroom can draw its conclusions at this point in the trial, but for the record, when you say "our partners," who were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the HVO, who formerly were partners in the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you to now look at Exhibits 218 and 219, which are next in your bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Chamber may recall these exhibits from before, so I will not go into them at length here. I think this witness has put them in further context by his testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring your attention first to P218, and this is the Charter of the Muslims of Herzegovina. Were you one of the persons who signed this document, sir, along with Mr. Demirovic and others?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And directing your attention to the Proclamation by the Muslims of Herzegovina, which is P219, did you also sign that proclamation?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think -- well, first of all, are these the documents that you were telling us about a few moments ago that were prepared by the Bosniak leadership in response to the ultimatums issued by Mr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think only one question concerning P218: Directing your attention to paragraph numbered 3, how was what you were stating here different than what you saw happening with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I did not understand. What item are you referring to at this point?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph number 3, which starts with the words "We are unwaveringly committed" -- this is 218.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in contrast to what the Bosniak leadership is communicating here, can you tell the Chamber what you saw in fact happening with the HVO at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I can explain it like this: Some proposals which were on the table, they wanted to pre-empt. They wanted to present them as foregone conclusions. They envisaged some provinces where they were -- where the Croats were in the majority and they wanted to make them exclusively Croatian provinces, and that is how they wanted to make arrangements. These -- there were a number of such proposals from the start of the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina. We did not want to consider them foregone conclusions, and we believed that first the war was to be concluded and then that these arrangements should be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to suggest -- these documents, I think, are quite rich, but I'll leave it to the Chamber's own questions, if they have any, to follow up in more detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when the 20th of January, 1993 came? What happened in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Nothing happened except that tensions continued. The escalation was drawn out until the 9th of May, when the Croatian side conducted an offensive against the Bosniak people. In other words, things were just put off. I think that it must have been political influences and/or political events which put things off for later. It is possible that Croats had expected that we wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I object to the answer at this point. This witness has answered this question. Now he is speculating, and this is improper for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll ask a follow-up question which -- frankly, all the witness has done is anticipate my next question, but I'll be happy to ask it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, we are happy with your first part of the answer. I think that's the answer of the question. Then the Prosecutor, if he has any doubts, he will continue his question and you just follow that pattern. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, in reference to the documents, the Charter of the Muslims and the Proclamation of the Muslims, both dated the 17th of January, 1993, did your community receive any satisfactory response or did conditions improve for the Bosniak community following those communications?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: There were no improvements, absolutely none, and no response was given -- was received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, that in fact after the 20th of January, 1993, in fact, violent confrontations did break out in such places as Gornji Vakuf, Busovaca, and other places between the Muslims and Bosniak community when the deadline passed?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I'm familiar with it, but my focus was really on the territory of Herzegovina. So in my mind, I simply did not focus on that area. But in this fall of 1992, there was a terrible conflict in Herzegovina, an unnecessary conflict in Prozor, where the Croatian forces carried out an actual massacre against the Bosniak side. This was as early as fall 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but I must object again. It's the same objection. My learned colleague asked the question of what happened after January 20, 1993, and this witness now is talking about fall of 1992. It's improper, and it does -- it's non-responsive. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you know the objections from the Defence counsel. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Further, Your Honour, please the Court, this last answer, we would respectfully request it be stricken. Prozor. These locations are not included within the context of our indictment whatsoever. Shouldn't be in the record. We ask it be stricken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, there should be very strict rules for those parts in the transcript being stricken. The Trial Chamber will make the proper judgement when we evaluate all this evidence. We will bear in mind your objections at this point. Thank you. Mr. Scott, would you please proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you briefly to tell us about an incident -- so your secretary -- was the car of your secretary seized by an HVO officer in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, by Mr. Misic, commander of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And let me, if I'm allowed, Mr. Smajkic, let me just ask some very specific questions about this, just to take this quite briefly. Your secretary was a man named Ihsan Mutevelic, M-u-t-e-v-e-l-i-c; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that when this gentleman went to protest the taking of his -- seizure of his car, that this HVO officer, Misic, put his pistol --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, please the Court, Your Honours, I have let this go all morning on background information, but this is very leading, it is very suggestive. If Mr. Scott wishes to testify, we should put him under oath and let him answer these questions. I strongly object to these type leading and suggestive questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've said all morning I'm happy to do it either way, and I'll ask the questions differently, if there is objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Please ask the questions in a different way because we come to the crucial point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I thought the testimony might move a bit quicker, if I did it that way, but I won't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened? What did Mr. Misic do to your secretary?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: When he went to protest with the commander of this battalion and ask of him to have his car brought back to him, he showed the documents pertaining to his being the secretary of the Mufti's office, and commander Misic placed a pistol in his mouth and abused him in a most aggressive way. He then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek? Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour. I don't know whether it's the English -- it's my headphone, but my headphone is cutting in and out real bad, all of a sudden, in the English, channel 4. The other ones, I notice, are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that my headphone is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mine is not, but I'll wait and see if it works. It keeps cutting in and out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll have Madam Registrar check it. I am not expecting any technical problems. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I can hear now, yes. It's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, to interrupt you. Will you please continue?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Misic abused my secretary in the worst way by placing a pistol in his mouth. He said that if he wanted the car brought back, that I should show up and talk to him directly. Of course, I didn't go, but he sent two policemen to my office to bring me to him. I found a way to avoid going there, and I eventually did not go, but the car stayed there. It was confiscated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just moving on, then, can you tell the Chamber anything about during the spring -- before May 9th -- just so we don't get ahead of ourselves, prior to the 9th of May, were any Bosniak intellectuals arrested in the Herzegovina area?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That was almost like a pogrom. Intellectuals from the Capljina and Stolac area were all rounded up through the months of February, March, April. All prominent Bosniak men were followed at that time and during that period, taken to be questioned by the police and curbed their activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it that curbed their activities?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: The HVO authority at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber approximately how many Bosniak intellectuals were treated in this way or detained during that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I know, because I was given information. I think that about 100 of these intellectuals from Stolac and Capljina, and educated men. These included physicians, engineers, lawyers. And they were mistreated in all kinds of ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move forward. Now, did you know or did -- did you become aware that in April, perhaps the end of March or early April, 1993, was there another round, if you will, of demands or ultimatum by the HVO leadership?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I know. I did not see these documents, but I know that it came to our leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't have that document, but I know that Mr. Izetbegovic and the military leadership received it from Mate Boban, the chief of the Croatian Defence Council. We were informed of it at that time, and we lived with it -- with anxiety. There were sniping incidents. There were arrests, beatings, detentions. And that unfortunate day was anticipated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before you go on, just so the record is clear, when you say Mr. Izetbegovic, is that the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I want you to look next at the next three items. I'll give you the exhibit number in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm referring now to Exhibit P288, P274, this is one of those instances where they are numerically out of order, but it's 288, 274 and 277. Perhaps in the interests of time, only 277, which is the third of those documents, is -- has attached a Serbo-Croatian language version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Smajkic, let me direct your attention to the Serbo-Croatian part of Exhibit 277. There is a box on that, appears to be a newspaper or a magazine article, and if you can just look at that portion, the title of that article -- and I won't attempt to read this, but it seems to indicate, "HVO, the ultimatum." I only say that to give you a point of reference. If you look at that - and perhaps the Chamber can look at the English translation obviously preceding that - can you just look at that and tell us is that what you're talking about in the last few minutes that you understood there had been another ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: That is exactly right. I did not see this, but that is the ultimatum that it refers to because it coincides with what was going on on the ground at that time, and I had some information, we were cut off from Sarajevo, but at that point we were seeking contact with Mr. Izetbegovic to figure out a way how to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Referring the Chamber's attention to paragraph -- excuse me, Exhibit P288. I'll just read this particular sentence to the witness in English. It will have to be translated obviously for him, but to put a question to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm looking on 288, Mr. Smajkic, to what would be the fifth paragraph, starting after the heading, the dateline, "Banja Luka, April 10th," the fifth paragraph: "Both Croats and Muslims, however, expect that the real conflict is yet to come after April 15th, the deadline set by Bosnian Croat leader Mate Boban for the withdrawal of all Muslim units from the so-called Croat provinces of the Vance-Owen Plan." And again, is that description of the events as they stood at that time consistent with your recollection of what you saw and heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this question because the witness had already stated that he never -- he had never seen this document. He is asked to come to make a comment on this newspaper report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked him to comment on the facts, not on the article itself. I suppose if I offered this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could rephrase your question, because the question you asked, in a way, gives some speculation of this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'll rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, do you recall yourself and the Bosniak leadership in the Mostar region at that time being aware there was something about a deadline about the 15th of April, and the expectation that things would become worse after that time, if you know. If you don't know, you don't know. If you do know, please assist us.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I know that we had contacts. We had just one cell phone at the time, and it was very difficult to communicate with Sarajevo. But I know that the tensions were pointing in that direction. And on the ground, there were already incidents such as mistreatment and sniping incidents which ended up in casualties, people being detained. I did not know the exact date, but that was a period which led to -- to full escalation, and we were trying to stop it. I, on my side, wanted to contribute to that, so I went and had a meeting with Bishop Peric and asked him to work on calming down things on his side. And it's in one of my documents, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I look at the clock. But if the Court would indulge us about maybe one or two minutes, we can finish, I think, on this point, and we can start on a new point after lunch. But he just went to this meeting with the Bishop Peric, and I would just like him to finish that, if he could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You went to a meeting with the Catholic Bishop Peric. And did anyone else go with you?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the other person who went was my secretary, and Mr. Demirovic also went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at the meeting? Why did you go to him?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: I did not see this document, but this is something the other document reflects. We had seen certain machine-guns being set up and positions being taken along the Bulevar that bisects the city, the two parts. And I went to the bishop and I said, "Why don't we put on our own uniforms, and why don't we just knock over those sandbags which had already been placed there, so that we give an example to people so that they could see how they should live and to prevent shooting." Because everything pointed to the fact that this moment was approaching.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say put on your uniforms, were you suggesting to the bishop that the two of you each put on your respective clerical clothing and go and tear down the sandbags as, essentially, a symbolic act? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Bishop Peric's response to your proposal?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC
utterances.text: Bishop Peric said that he could not do it, that this was a military and political matter, and he could do nothing in that regard. We were not happy with that answer so we went to the provincial of Herzegovina, Mr. Tole [phoen], the same group. And we also invited some people from that neighbourhood, Podhum, who personally knew some of these religious personnel there. We said that this was inevitably leading to conflict and that the church should do something in regard of that proposal which I had given to Bishop Peric. And, unfortunately, we received the same answer as from Bishop Peric, that we should not meddle in this, this is not our matter, a matter for us. We are a people of faith and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can end there, please. Thank you for the extra minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber was just informed by the Detention Unit that Mr. Naletilic will not be able to be present this afternoon. He is going to be seen by a physician. So Mr. Krsnik, we would like to ask your opinion concerning sitting this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am a little worried. My request was to go myself to the Detention Unit. I have been with my client for years now. I know what his health condition is. I know all the treatments that he has undergone. I am worried because he has not come back, and I know how much he desires to be present during the hearing. When I talked to him last time, he had no feeling in the whole left side. He had no grip in his left hand. So it could be potentially very serious. Of course, I'm not a physician. I cannot give any opinions. My intention was to go there. Of course, I would say I would like to go on, but this is an extraordinary situation. This just took place about half an hour ago. With your permission, Your Honour, I don't think that we will be able to finish this witness today, as far as I can see. My learned colleague still has some more examination-in-chief to conduct. And with your permission, I would really like to go to the Detention Unit and check on my client. And that is my reason for asking for -- or in the alternative, I don't know. Perhaps maybe we can start at 3.00. Maybe that will give me enough time to come back. But then I don't know. I'm in your hands, really. But the fact is that we will have to deal with the witness into tomorrow. But I'm in your hands, and I will abide by any ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This Trial Chamber realises that this witness is an essential one to this case. We should have heard him at the beginning of this trial. We also notice that in the past sittings, Mr. Naletilic was actively participating in the proceedings by the frequent communications with his counsel. Taking into consideration the condition of Mr. Naletilic's health, as well as to the fairness -- for the fairness to the accused and his Defence team, we have reached the conclusion that we will not sit this afternoon so that to let Mr. Krsnik to have enough time to go to the Detention Unit to see the condition of Mr. Naletilic. Thank you. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 1.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of October, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 23 24 25
